definition: A unit of ownership in a company. Owning shares makes you a part-owner (shareholder) of that company.
example: If a company has 1,000 shares and you own 25, you own 2.5% of it.

definition: A person or organisation that owns shares in a company. Ordinary shareholders can usually vote at the general meeting and may receive dividends.
Ownership in a company. In investing, "equities" is the formal word for stocks. On a balance sheet, equity is what belongs to the owners: assets minus liabilities.
A payment a company makes to its shareholders, usually out of its profits. Dividends are not guaranteed: the company decides whether to pay one and how much.
example: A company pays a dividend of €2 per share. If you own 50 shares, you receive €100 (before taxes).

definition: The profit you make when you sell an investment for more than you paid for it. Selling for less than you paid is a capital loss.
example: You buy a share for €80 and sell it for €100: a capital gain of €20 (before fees and taxes).

definition: The total market value of a company's shares: the share price multiplied by the number of shares.
example: 1,000,000 shares at €50 each = a market capitalisation of €50 million.

definition: The meeting of a company's shareholders, usually held once a year, where shareholders can vote on important matters such as electing board members or approving a dividend.
Spreading your money across many different investments (for example many companies, sectors and countries) so that a problem with one of them does less damage to the whole.
A debt security: a loan from an investor to a company or government. The issuer pays interest during the bond's life and repays the face value when it matures.
example: You buy a 5-year bond for €1,000 paying 4% a year: you receive €40 interest each year and €1,000 back after 5 years, if the issuer can pay.

definition: Money that is borrowed and must be paid back, usually with interest. For a company, loans and bonds are debt; for an investor, buying a bond means lending money (holding debt).
A person or organisation that is owed money, for example a bank that gave a loan or an investor who holds a bond. Creditors are paid before shareholders if a company is liquidated.
The price of borrowing money, shown as a percentage per year. Borrowers pay it; lenders and savers receive it.
example: €1,000 at an interest rate of 3% earns €30 in one year.

definition: Where new securities are issued for the first time and the issuer (a company or government) receives the money, for example in an IPO.
Where investors trade existing securities with each other, for example on a stock exchange. The company that issued the shares does not receive money from these trades.
Initial public offering: the first time a company sells its shares to the public and has them listed on a stock exchange.
The rule that shareholders of companies such as an AG are not personally liable for the company's debts. The most a shareholder can lose is what they paid for their shares.
A type of share that usually has no voting rights but receives dividends before ordinary shares and ranks ahead of them if the company is liquidated.
A tradable investment instrument, such as a stock or a bond.
A short code, usually a few letters, that a stock exchange uses for a listed security. Tickers are not unique across exchanges.
A 12-character code that identifies one security worldwide: a 2-letter country code, a 9-character basic number and a check digit. In Austria, ISINs are assigned by the OeKB.
A six-character German securities identification code. It has largely been replaced by the ISIN but is still widely used in German-speaking countries.
An organised, regulated marketplace where securities of listed companies are traded under fixed rules. Today trading is almost entirely electronic.
Under the EU's MiFID II rules: a regulated market, a multilateral trading facility (MTF) or an organised trading facility (OTF).
Multilateral trading facility: an EU trading venue, run by an investment firm or market operator, that brings many buyers and sellers together under fixed rules, similar to an exchange.
Over-the-counter: trading directly between two parties instead of on a trading venue. In the US, 'OTC securities' are securities not listed on a national securities exchange.
A number that tracks the prices of a selected group of shares, such as Austria's ATX. News reports often call it 'the market'.
A private person who buys and sells investments with their own money, for themselves.
A professional organisation that pools money and invests it on behalf of others, such as pension funds, investment funds, insurance companies and banks.
A firm that stands ready to buy or sell a security at publicly quoted prices, making it easier for others to trade at any time.
A firm that buys and sells securities on behalf of its clients and usually holds them in the client's account. Retail investors reach the market through a broker.
A general rise in prices over time, which means the same amount of money buys less.
example: If prices rise 3% in a year, something that cost €100 now costs €103.

definition: How strongly and how often an investment's price moves up and down. More volatile means bigger swings in both directions.
A group of investments that behave in similar ways, such as stocks, bonds, cash or property.
The money (or other assets) that owners contribute to a corporation in exchange for shares. In an Austrian AG it is called Grundkapital and is divided into shares.
The German and Austrian name for a stock corporation: a company with its own legal personality whose share capital is divided into shares. In Austria the minimum share capital is €70,000.

Gesellschaft mit beschränkter Haftung: a limited liability company common in Austria, Germany and Switzerland. In Austria it needs at least €10,000 of share capital; its ownership stakes are not traded on stock exchanges.
Austria's commercial register. A GmbH or AG only comes into existence when it is entered in the Firmenbuch.
The nominal amount printed on a share (in Austria at least €1 for par value shares). It is an accounting figure and says nothing about the market price.
A share without a nominal amount; each share represents an equal fraction of the share capital.
A share whose owner is recorded by name in the company's share register. In Austria, unlisted AGs must issue registered shares.
A share whose owner is not recorded by name in a company register.
The company's list of the names of holders of registered shares. In Austria (Aktienbuch), only the person entered counts as a shareholder towards the company.
The maximum number of shares a company is allowed to issue under its founding documents. Issued shares are those actually handed out.
Capitalisation table: a list of everyone who holds a company's shares and related securities (such as options and convertible notes), with how many and on which terms.
The reduction in existing owners' percentage when a company issues new shares. Owners keep the same number of shares, but each is a smaller slice.
example: You own 100 of 1,000 shares (10%). The company issues 250 new shares: you now own 100 of 1,250 (8%).

definition: What a company is considered to be worth, as estimated by analysts or agreed between a company and its investors.
A company's value before new money from a funding round is added.
A company's value right after a funding round: pre-money valuation plus the new money. The investor's share equals the investment divided by the post-money valuation.
example: €4 million pre-money + €1 million investment = €5 million post-money; the investor owns €1m ÷ €5m = 20%.

definition: A wealthy individual who invests their own money directly in young companies, typically in early funding rounds.
Money from venture capital (VC) funds: private funds that invest in fast-growing young companies in exchange for equity, usually preferred shares.
Typically a company's first formal funding round, often from friends and family, angel investors or early-stage funds, frequently using convertible notes or SAFEs.
A later funding round, named in order (Series A, Series B, Series C...), often led by venture capital funds.
A loan to a young company that converts into shares (usually preferred shares) at a later funding round or other agreed event. Common in seed rounds.
Often shortened to SAFE: an agreement in which a company promises an investor shares in the future if certain events happen, such as a later funding round.
An investor's right to be paid before other shareholders when the company is sold or wound up, often expressed as a multiple of the investment (1x, 2x).
The right, but not the obligation, to buy a certain number of the company's shares at a fixed price (the strike price), usually after a vesting period.
The process by which an employee gradually earns the right to stock options or shares, for example by staying with the company for a set time.
Raising money from many private individuals, each investing small amounts, usually through an online platform. Investments are often unsecured and carry a high risk of loss.
The official offering document for a public offer of securities, describing the company, its business, finances, risks and the terms of the offer. In Austria it must be approved by the FMA.
An investment bank that manages and sells a securities offering such as an IPO for the issuing company. The lead bank is often called the bookrunner.
Collecting investors' orders (how many shares, up to what price) during an offer's subscription period, to help set the final offer price.
A series of presentations in which a company's management presents an offer to potential investors.
An option allowing the underwriting banks to buy additional shares at the offer price to cover over-allotted shares. Under EU rules it may not exceed 15% of the original offer.
Purchases by the underwriting banks after an offer to support the share price. In the EU, for a share IPO it must end within 30 calendar days and never above the offer price.
An agreement that stops company insiders and large shareholders from selling their shares for a period after an IPO. Most US lock-ups last 180 days, though terms vary.
In the US, the period around the registration of an offering when the company must make sure its public communications about the offer comply with securities laws.
When investors order more shares in an offer than are available, so orders have to be scaled down.
Newly issued shares sold in an offering; the money goes to the company.
Existing shares sold in an offering by current owners; the money goes to those sellers, not to the company.
Admitting a company's existing shares to trading on an exchange without a traditional underwritten IPO; the opening price is found by the market.
Special purpose acquisition company: a shell company with no business of its own that goes public, raises money and then merges with a private company (the de-SPAC transaction).
A way of going public in which a private company merges into an existing listed shell company and takes it over, without a traditional IPO.
When a company separates a division into a new, independent company and gives the new company's shares to its own shareholders.
The part of a company's shares that is available for trading by the public, excluding long-term holdings of founders, families, governments or strategic owners.
When an IPO's offer price is set below the price at which the shares start trading, giving IPO buyers an immediate gain.
Selling shares received in an IPO immediately after trading starts.
An institution that records securities in an electronic book-entry system and keeps them safe. In Austria: OeKB CSD.
Holding securities as electronic account entries instead of paper certificates. Ownership changes by changing the entries.
A bank or firm that holds securities in safekeeping for its clients.
When a company issues new shares to raise money. Existing shareholders are diluted unless they buy their share of the new shares.
A capital increase in which existing shareholders get the first right to buy the new shares, in proportion to what they already own.
A procedure that lets a majority shareholder force the remaining minority shareholders out against a cash payment. In Austria the threshold is 90%.
When a company's shares are removed from a stock exchange. The shares still exist, but become much harder to trade.
When one company or investor acquires control of another company, usually by buying most or all of its shares.
The standard type of share: it usually carries a vote at the general meeting and a share in dividends, and ranks last in a liquidation.
A category of a company's shares with its own rights, for example different votes or dividends (Class A, Class B). The letters have no standard meaning.
A setup in which founders or insiders hold shares with more votes per share than the shares sold to the public, so they can control the company with a minority of the shares.
A share of a company whose earnings are growing faster than the market average. Growth companies rarely pay dividends and reinvest their profits.
A share that looks cheap compared with the company's earnings (for example a low P/E ratio), often because it is out of favour with investors.
A share of a company that pays dividends consistently; investors buy it mainly for regular income.
A share of a large, well-known company with a long and solid history, which generally pays dividends.
A share of a company whose sales and profits rise and fall strongly with the economy, such as car makers or airlines.
A share of a company whose products people keep buying even in a recession, such as food, household goods or utilities, so its profits tend to be steadier.
A company with a very large market capitalisation. There is no single official threshold.
A smaller listed company by market capitalisation. Small caps can grow faster but tend to be more volatile and less followed.
A very small listed company. In the US the term is often used for companies worth less than about $250–300 million. Microcaps can be illiquid and are frequent targets of fraud.
A share with a very low price. Such companies may have little or no earnings, rarely pay dividends and are highly speculative.
A share whose price is driven mainly by social-media excitement among individual investors rather than by the business, such as GameStop in January 2021.
A broad area of the economy, such as energy, health care or financials, used to group similar companies.

Global Industry Classification Standard: a system created in 1999 by S&P Dow Jones Indices and MSCI that classifies companies into 11 sectors, 25 industry groups, 74 industries and 163 sub-industries.
American depositary receipt: a certificate traded in the US in dollars that represents shares of a non-US company held by a US depositary bank.
Global depositary receipt: like an ADR, a receipt representing shares of a company, generally offered to investors in more than one country.
Real estate investment trust: a company that owns and typically operates income-producing real estate or related assets. Most REITs pay out most of their income as dividends.
Usually a bond or preferred share that can be converted into a different security, typically the company's common shares.
A security giving the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell an underlying asset at a fixed price within or at the end of a set period. Warrants can expire worthless.
The right of existing shareholders to buy new shares in a capital increase before others, in proportion to their holdings. It protects against dilution and can often be traded.
In Austria and Germany, a bond issued by a bank whose payout depends on an underlying asset such as a share or index. You lend money to the issuer and carry its credit risk.
Less than one whole share, bought through brokers that offer fractional share investing. Voting rights, fees and transferability depend on the broker.
U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission: the federal authority that regulates the US securities markets and runs the investor education site Investor.gov.
Finanzmarktaufsicht: Austria's Financial Market Authority, which supervises banks, insurers, investment firms and the securities markets in Austria.
European Securities and Markets Authority: the EU authority that works on common rules and supervisory practice for securities markets across the EU.
The list of all buy and sell orders for a security that are waiting to be executed, sorted by price and time.
The price at which someone is willing to buy. The highest bid in the order book is the best bid.
The price at which someone is willing to sell, also called the offer. The lowest ask in the order book is the best ask.
The difference between the best ask (lowest selling price) and the best bid (highest buying price). A narrow spread usually signals a liquid security.
example: Best bid €10.00, best ask €10.02: the spread is €0.02.

definition: The rule for sorting orders: the best price comes first, and among orders at the same price, the earliest one comes first.
The exchange's computer system that matches buy and sell orders according to its rules.
How quickly and easily a security can be bought or sold without substantially moving its price.
The process by which many buy and sell orders meeting in a market produce a price.
A trading mode in which orders are collected during a call phase and then executed together at the single price where the largest number of shares can be traded.
The auction at the end of the trading day that determines the official closing price.
A trading mode in which each incoming order is immediately checked against the order book and executed if possible.
The EU term for a classic stock exchange: an authorised multilateral system bringing buyers and sellers together under non-discretionary rules.
A trading system where participants place orders without publicly displaying their size and price, used mainly by institutions to trade large orders.
In the US, an SEC-regulated electronic system that matches orders for securities but is not registered as a national securities exchange.
An EU investment firm that trades against its clients' orders on its own account, outside a trading venue, on a frequent and substantial basis.
Everything between a trade and its final settlement: confirming details, working out obligations and managing the risk that a side fails.
The final exchange of a trade: securities move to the buyer and money to the seller, usually at a central securities depository.
An institution that steps into trades as the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer, so that one side's default does not hit the other. In Vienna: CCP Austria.
A settlement method in which securities are delivered only if payment is made, and the other way round, so neither side is left exposed.
The time between the trade date (T) and settlement, such as T+1 or T+2 business days. The US uses T+1 since May 2024; the EU moves from T+2 to T+1 on 11 October 2027.
A rule that halts trading when prices fall or move too far, too fast. In the US, market-wide halts are triggered by S&P 500 falls of 7%, 13% and 20%.
On Xetra-based markets such as Vienna: a short switch from continuous trading into an auction when the next price would fall outside a set price corridor.
A temporary stop in trading of a security, for example while important news is pending.
The smallest step by which a price can change. In the EU it depends on a share's price and liquidity.
The minimum quantity, or multiple, in which a security can be traded in some markets.
Trading in which computer programs automatically decide on orders, such as when, at what price and in what quantity.
The fastest form of algorithmic trading, using infrastructure such as co-location to minimise delays, automated decisions and very high numbers of orders and cancellations.
Placing a trading firm's computers inside or next to an exchange's data centre to reduce the time orders take to arrive.
The fixed times, in local time, during which an exchange is open for trading, usually split into auctions and continuous trading.
Trading before the official opening of the regular session, mainly offered in the US. Liquidity is lower and spreads are wider.
Trading after the regular session closes, also called extended-hours trading. Prices can swing strongly on few trades.
On the Vienna Stock Exchange, a short phase after the closing auction in which orders can be executed at the official closing price.
A weekday on which an exchange is closed. Exchange holidays do not always match public holidays.
A shortened trading day, for example the NYSE closing at 1:00 p.m. on the day after Thanksgiving and on Christmas Eve.
Moving clocks forward one hour in summer. The EU switches on the last Sundays of March and October; the US on the second Sunday of March and the first Sunday of November.
The hours when two major markets are open at the same time, such as Europe and the US (normally 15:30–17:30 Vienna time).
The third Friday of March, June, September and December, when stock options, stock index futures and options on those futures expire together in the US.
The day on which a futures or options contract ends and is settled. For many European index derivatives it is the third Friday of the contract month.
The regular review of an index, in which members are added or removed and weights adjusted; index funds then have to buy and sell accordingly.
Trading during the night, outside regular and early/late sessions. US exchanges are preparing near-continuous '23/5' trading.
The account in which a bank or broker holds your securities. In Austria and Germany it is called a Depot. The securities in it belong to you.
An app-first online broker with a simple interface and often very low or no commission per trade. Total costs and order routing vary.
The duty of financial firms to verify a customer's identity and know essential facts about them, for example to prevent money laundering and fraud.
Under MiFID II, the check a firm must make before giving advice or managing a portfolio: your knowledge and experience, financial situation and ability to bear losses, objectives and risk tolerance.
Under MiFID II, the check whether a client has the knowledge and experience to understand the risks of a product when it is bought without advice; if not, the firm must warn the client.
A securities account in which you can only buy with your own money, so you cannot lose more than you put in.
A securities account in which the broker lends you money to buy securities, using your account as collateral. It magnifies gains and losses.
A demand from a broker to add money or securities to a margin account after prices have fallen. The broker can also sell your securities, possibly without notice.
Individual Savings Account: a UK account in which savings and investments grow free of UK tax, up to an annual allowance (£20,000 in the 2026/27 tax year).
US retirement accounts with tax advantages. For 2026, contribution limits are $7,500 for an IRA and $24,500 for a 401(k).
Nippon Individual Savings Account: Japan's tax-exempt investment account.
Tax-Free Savings Account: a Canadian account in which interest, dividends and capital gains are generally tax-free, even on withdrawal; contributions are not tax-deductible.
An order to buy or sell immediately at the best available price. It guarantees execution, but not the price.
An order to buy at or below, or sell at or above, a set price. It guarantees the price (or better), but not execution.
The difference between the price you expected when placing an order and the price at which it was actually executed.
When only part of an order is executed because not enough shares are available at the acceptable price.
An order that becomes a market order when a set stop price is reached. A sell stop below the current price is used to limit losses (stop-loss).
An order that becomes a limit order when a stop price is reached. It protects the price but may not execute at all.
A stop order whose stop price follows the market price at a set distance as the price moves favourably, but does not move back.
An order valid only for the trading day it is entered; if not executed, it is generally cancelled at the end of regular trading hours.
An order that stays open until it is executed or cancelled (brokers usually set a maximum period).
An order that must be executed immediately; any part that cannot be filled at once is cancelled.
An order that must be executed immediately and in full, otherwise it is cancelled completely.
Investing a fixed amount automatically at regular intervals, for example monthly, often in an ETF or fund.
Investing the same amount regularly means buying more units when prices are low and fewer when they are high, which lowers the average cost per unit compared with the average price.
Lending securities to another party for a period against collateral and a fee; the borrower returns securities of the same kind and number. Often used for short selling.
Payments a broker receives from a trading firm for sending client orders to it. It creates a conflict of interest and is banned in the EU (fully since 30 June 2026).
The EU duty of investment firms to take sufficient steps to obtain the best possible result for clients when executing orders; for retail clients, measured by total cost.
Protection of bank deposits if a bank fails: in the EU, up to €100,000 per person per bank. In Austria it also covers securities clearing accounts, but not the securities themselves.
Compensation if a bank or investment firm cannot return clients' securities or money owed from securities business; in Austria up to €20,000 per investor. It does not cover market losses.
Selling borrowed shares in the hope of buying them back later at a lower price. Losses are theoretically unlimited if the price rises.
A gain or loss on an investment you still hold (a 'paper' gain or loss). It becomes realised when you sell.
The first day a share trades without the right to the upcoming dividend. The share price usually drops by about the dividend amount on this day.
The last day on which a share can be bought with the right to the upcoming dividend.
The day on which the holdings in securities accounts determine who receives a dividend.
The day a dividend is actually paid out to shareholders.
A one-off dividend paid outside the regular schedule, for example after selling a business.
The annual dividend per share divided by the share price, in percent.
The share of a company's profit paid out as dividends: dividends ÷ net profit (or dividend per share ÷ earnings per share).
The full return of an investment: price change plus income such as dividends, usually assuming income is reinvested.
Interest (or returns) earned on both the original amount and on earlier interest. End value = start value × (1 + rate)^years.
A shortcut for doubling time: 72 divided by the yearly return in percent gives the approximate number of years to double.
The return in money terms, before accounting for inflation.
The return after inflation, showing the change in purchasing power: (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1.
Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices: the measure of inflation used by the ECB for the euro area.
The yearly costs charged to a fund (management, custody, audit and other fees) as a percentage of its assets.
A fee charged for keeping your securities account, often a percentage per year or a fixed amount.
The selling price at which you get back exactly what you paid, including all costs of buying and selling.
A pool of money from many investors that is invested together in shares, bonds or other assets. Each investor owns units of the whole portfolio.
The value of a fund's assets minus its liabilities, usually expressed per unit. Traditional funds are bought and sold at a price based on it.
example: Assets of €10m, liabilities of €50,000 and 1,000,000 units give a NAV of €9.95 per unit.

definition: A fund that aims to track an index as closely as possible instead of picking investments, usually at lower cost than an active fund.
A fund whose manager selects investments with the aim of beating a benchmark index, usually charging higher fees than an index fund.
An index used as a yardstick to judge a fund's or portfolio's performance.
A fund whose units trade on a stock exchange throughout the day like shares. Most ETFs track an index.

aliases: Undertakings for Collective Investment in Transferable Securities
definition: The EU's main legal framework for funds that are easily accessible to retail investors. UCITS funds follow common EU rules; being a UCITS does not make a fund safe.
A large financial institution allowed to create and redeem ETF units directly with the fund in large blocks. Its trading helps keep the ETF price close to its NAV.
The process by which authorised participants exchange baskets of securities (or cash) for new ETF units (creation), or return units to the fund (redemption).
When an ETF's market price is above (premium) or below (discount) the value of its holdings. Usually small for liquid ETFs; can widen in stressed markets.
Tracking an index by actually holding the shares in it, either all of them in index weight (full replication) or a representative selection (sampling).
A form of physical replication in which a fund holds a representative selection of an index's members rather than all of them.
Tracking an index through a swap with a bank that promises to pay the index return, while the fund holds a different basket of securities. Adds counterparty risk.
The risk that the other party to a contract, such as a swap, cannot meet its obligations.
A fund that reinvests the income it receives instead of paying it out, so the value of each unit grows. In Austria the reinvested income is still taxed yearly.
A fund that pays out the income it receives (such as dividends) to its investors, typically several times a year.
The difference between a fund's return and the return of the index it tracks over a period. Mainly driven by costs.
example: Index +8.0%, fund +7.8%: tracking difference −0.2 percentage points.

definition: Strictly, how much a fund's deviation from its index fluctuates over time. Also used loosely for any deviation from the index.
Index strategies that select or weight shares by characteristics such as value, momentum, low volatility or dividends instead of market value alone.
An ETF that invests in companies linked to a theme, such as robotics or clean energy. Often concentrated and more expensive than broad index funds.
A product that aims for a multiple (for example 2× or 3×) of an index's daily return. Because it resets daily, results over longer periods can differ greatly from that multiple.
example: Index +10% then −10% (−1% overall): a 2× product goes +20% then −20%, −4% overall.

definition: A product that aims for the opposite of an index's daily return. Over longer periods its results can differ greatly from the inverse of the index's return.
An index in which each member's weight is its market value divided by the total market value of all members. Most major indexes work this way.
An index in which members count according to their share price, regardless of company size, such as the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the Nikkei 225.
An index in which every member counts the same, regardless of size.
The Vienna Stock Exchange's leading index of about 20 of the most liquid Austrian shares, weighted by market value.
Germany's leading share index of the 40 largest and highest-turnover German shares on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange's regulated market.
A US index of 500 leading companies covering about 80% of the available US market capitalisation, weighted by free-float market value.
A price-weighted index of 30 US blue-chip companies.
A price-weighted index of 225 stocks in the Prime Market of the Tokyo Stock Exchange.
A global index of large and mid-sized companies in developed markets only; it does not include emerging markets.
A global index of large and mid-sized companies in both developed and emerging markets.
Countries whose economies and financial markets are still developing, such as China or India; index providers classify which countries count.
A short, standardised document for EU retail investors that describes a product's objectives, risks and costs.
Austria's tax on capital income such as dividends, price gains and fund income, generally 27.5% for shares and funds. Usually withheld by an Austrian custodian.
A fund that reports its tax data to the OeKB, Austria's official reporting office, so that banks can calculate KESt on its income correctly.
Under Austrian law, fund income that is not paid out but is treated as if it had been distributed, so it is taxed every year. It increases the tax acquisition cost of the units.
Oesterreichische Kontrollbank, which among other roles is Austria's official reporting office for fund tax data and the national ISIN agency.
The amount paid for an investment, used to work out the gain or loss when it is sold. Tax rules define exactly what counts; in Austria, taxed deemed distributed income from a fund increases it.
The price per share at which shares are sold to investors in an IPO or other public offer, set by the company with its banks at the end of bookbuilding.
example: BAWAG's 2017 IPO had a price range of €47 to €52 and an offer price of €48.

definition: The last price of a trading period, usually set in the closing auction. Line charts connect closing prices, and most indicators are calculated from them.
Analysing price charts, volume and indicators to describe what the market has been doing, often with the aim of anticipating future moves. Its usefulness is debated.
A chart symbol showing a period's open, high, low and close: a thick body between open and close and thin wicks up to the high and down to the low.
example: Open 100, high 106, low 98, close 104: a rising candle with a body from 100 to 104.

definition: Open, high, low and close: the four prices of a trading period shown by candlesticks and bar charts.
The thin line above or below a candle's body, reaching the period's high or low. Also called a shadow. A long wick shows that prices were pushed back.
Smoothed candles built from averages of the current and previous period. They make trends easier to see but do not show prices that actually traded.
A price axis on which equal distances mean equal percentage changes (10 to 20 looks as big as 100 to 200). Useful for long periods.
The period each candle or bar represents, such as 5 minutes, 1 hour, 1 day or 1 week. The same market can look very different on different timeframes.
A candle whose open and close are (almost) equal, so the body is a thin line: a sign of indecision.
A candle with a small body in the middle and wicks on both sides longer than the body: indecision.
A candle with a long body and no (or tiny) wicks: one side was in control from open to close.
After a decline, a candle with a small body near the top and a long lower wick (or, for the inverted hammer, a long upper wick). Traditionally read as a possible bullish reversal.
The same shape as a hammer (small body on top, long lower wick) but after a rise. Traditionally read as a bearish warning, though it often fails.
After a rise, a candle with a small body near the bottom and a long upper wick. Traditionally read as a possible bearish reversal.
Two candles where the second body completely covers the first body of the opposite colour. Traditionally read as a possible reversal.
Two candles where a small body sits inside the previous long body of the opposite colour: the move has paused. Japanese for 'pregnant'.
A two-candle pattern after a decline: a falling candle, then a rising one that opens below its low and closes above the middle of its body. The bearish mirror image is called dark cloud cover.
A three-candle pattern after a decline: a long falling candle, a small 'star', then a long rising candle. The evening star is its bearish mirror image after a rise.
Three long rising candles in a row, each closing near its high. The bearish mirror image (three long falling candles) is called three black crows.
de: Three White Soldiers / Three Black Crows

definition: Two candles with (almost) the same high (tweezer top) or the same low (tweezer bottom): the price failed twice at the same level.
A candle whose high and low are both within the previous candle's range: the market is pausing and the range is contracting.
An empty space on a chart when a period opens far above or below the previous period's range, often after news. Types: area, breakaway, continuation and exhaustion gaps.
A series of higher highs and higher lows (uptrend) or lower highs and lower lows (downtrend).
A line drawn through two or more lows (in an uptrend) or highs (in a downtrend) to show the slope of a trend. A parallel second line forms a channel.
Support: a price area where a falling price has tended to stop. Resistance: an area where a rising price has tended to stop. Best treated as zones, not exact lines.
A decisive move beyond a support or resistance zone or a chart pattern. A false breakout (fakeout) quickly falls back inside.
A reversal chart pattern: a high, a higher high and a lower high, with a neckline through the lows between them. A break of the neckline is the traditional signal.
Two highs (or lows, for a double bottom) at about the same level. Traders usually wait for a break of the price between them.
Continuation patterns in which the price range narrows (triangles, pennants) or pauses against a sharp move (flags) before a possible breakout.
The average price of the last n periods, recalculated each period (simple), or with more weight on recent prices (exponential). It smooths the price but lags.
example: Closes of 45.50, 45.25 and 46.10 give a 3-period SMA of 45.62.

definition: When the 50-day moving average crosses above the 200-day average (golden cross) or below it (death cross). Both lag the actual turn in price.
Relative Strength Index: compares average gains with average losses over a period (often 14) on a scale of 0 to 100. Readings above 70 are conventionally called overbought, below 30 oversold.
Moving Average Convergence Divergence: the 12-period EMA minus the 26-period EMA, with a 9-period signal line and a histogram of the difference.
An indicator drawn in its own pane that moves within a range or around zero, such as RSI or MACD.
A moving average (by default 20 periods) with bands two standard deviations above and below it. The bands widen when volatility rises and narrow when it falls.
Volume-weighted average price: the average price of a session weighted by how much traded at each price. It restarts every session.
Average True Range: the average size of each period's range, including gaps from the previous close. A measure of volatility, not direction.
Lines at 38.2%, 50% and 61.8% of a previous move, where some traders expect a pullback to pause. Popular but subjective.
Reading the same market on several timeframes, from long (weekly) to short (hourly), to see the context before the detail.
Testing how a set of trading rules would have performed on past data. Prone to overfitting, data snooping, survivorship bias and ignoring costs.
Adjusting or selecting trading rules until they fit past data very well, so they capture noise and usually fail on new data.
A distortion that arises when only the survivors (companies or funds that still exist) are studied, ignoring those that failed, which makes results look better.
Practising trades in a simulated account with virtual money. Useful for learning, but without real emotions or real execution.
The idea that prices quickly reflect available information, so past prices are of little use for predicting short-term returns.
Judging a company and its shares from the business itself: financial statements, profits, cash, debt, competition and management, rather than from price charts.

A listed company's yearly report with the audited financial statements, the management report and other information. In Austria, listed companies must publish an annual financial report within four months of the year end.
A snapshot of what a company owns (assets), owes (liabilities) and what is left for the owners (shareholders' equity) on one date. Assets always equal liabilities plus equity.
The financial statement that shows a company's revenue, costs and profit or loss over a period, from sales at the top to net income at the bottom.
The financial statement that shows cash coming in and going out over a period, split into operating, investing and financing activities.
The part of an annual report in which management explains the business, results, outlook and main risks. The US equivalent in a 10-K is the MD&A (management's discussion and analysis).
What would be left for the owners if a company sold all its assets at their balance sheet values and paid all its liabilities. Also called book value.
Current assets minus current liabilities: roughly the short-term money a company has to run its day-to-day business.
Current assets divided by current liabilities. It shows how well short-term obligations are covered by assets that should turn into cash within a year.
Current assets minus inventory, divided by current liabilities. A stricter version of the current ratio that leaves out inventory, which may be hard to sell quickly.
The value of shareholders' equity as shown on the balance sheet. Divided by the number of shares it gives book value per share.
An intangible asset that arises when a company buys another company for more than the fair value of its identifiable net assets. It is tested for impairment under IFRS.
A write-down when an asset, such as goodwill or a factory, is worth less than the value it is carried at on the balance sheet. It reduces profit and equity.
Interest-bearing debt minus cash. It shows how much debt would remain if a company used all its cash to repay it. Definitions vary, for example on leases.
Gross profit (revenue minus cost of sales) as a percentage of revenue.
Operating profit as a percentage of revenue: how much of each euro of sales is left after operating costs.
Earnings before interest and taxes: roughly a company's operating profit, before the effects of financing and tax.

aliases: earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation
earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization
definition: Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation. EBIT with depreciation and amortisation added back. Not defined by IFRS, so companies calculate it differently.
The profit or loss at the bottom of the income statement, after all costs, interest and taxes. Also called net profit or net earnings.
Net income divided by the number of shares. Under IFRS, companies show basic EPS and diluted EPS, which assumes options and convertibles become shares.

Spreading the cost of long-lived assets over the years they are used: depreciation for physical assets such as machines, amortisation for intangible assets. A cost in the income statement that does not use cash in that year.
Cash spent on long-term assets such as buildings, machines and software. Shown under investing activities in the cash flow statement.
Cash generated by a company's day-to-day business in a period: net income adjusted for non-cash items and changes in working capital.
Cash left after a company pays for the investment it needs, often calculated as operating cash flow minus capital expenditure. Not defined by IFRS, so definitions vary.
Net income divided by shareholders' equity: the profit earned on the owners' book capital. Debt can make it look higher.
Net income divided by total assets: profit earned on everything the company owns.
After-tax operating profit divided by the capital provided by shareholders and lenders (debt plus equity minus cash). A business creates value when it is above its cost of capital.
Splitting return on equity into net margin × asset turnover × financial leverage, to see whether a high ROE comes from profitability, efficiency or debt.
Debt compared with shareholders' equity. Some sources use total liabilities, others only interest-bearing debt.
Shareholders' equity as a percentage of total assets. A common measure of financial strength in German-speaking countries.
Operating profit (EBIT) divided by interest expense: how many times profit covers the interest bill.
Cost of sales divided by average inventory: how many times a year a company sells through its stock.
Share price divided by earnings per share: how many euros investors pay for one euro of annual profit. Meaningless when earnings are negative.
The price-earnings ratio calculated with forecast earnings for the next year instead of reported earnings.
The P/E ratio divided by the expected yearly earnings growth rate in percent. It depends heavily on a growth forecast.
Share price divided by book value per share. Most useful for companies whose assets are close to market value, such as banks.
Market capitalisation divided by revenue. Used for companies without profits, but sales are not profits.
The value of the whole business to shareholders and lenders: market value of equity plus debt minus cash.
Enterprise value divided by EBITDA. A valuation ratio that compares companies with different debt levels more fairly than the P/E.
Earnings per share divided by the share price: the P/E ratio turned upside down, expressed as a percentage.
A share that looks cheap on ratios such as a low P/E but stays cheap or falls further, because the business is in lasting decline.
An estimate of what a business is worth based on the cash it can produce over its remaining life, discounted to today. Always an estimate, not a precise figure.
A valuation method that forecasts a company's future cash flows and discounts them to today's value. Small changes in assumptions can change the result a lot.
What a future payment is worth today: the future amount divided by (1 + discount rate) for each year of waiting.
In valuation, the yearly return used to convert future cash flows into today's value; higher risk means a higher discount rate. Some central banks also use the term for one of their lending rates.
In a DCF, the value of all cash flows after the detailed forecast years, usually estimated with a constant growth rate. It often makes up most of the result.
Buying only when the price is well below the estimated value, as a buffer against errors in the estimate. A principle associated with Benjamin Graham.
A durable competitive advantage, such as a strong brand or low costs, that protects a company's high returns from competitors.
Michael Porter's framework for industry profitability: rivalry, customers, suppliers, potential new entrants and substitute products.
A financial figure that is not defined by the accounting standards, such as EBITDA, adjusted profit or net debt. ESMA expects companies to define and reconcile them.
International Financial Reporting Standards, issued by the IASB. EU-listed groups must use them, as adopted by the EU, for their consolidated accounts.
European Single Electronic Format: the machine-readable format (Inline XBRL) in which EU-listed companies must publish their annual financial reports.
The independent auditor's opinion on whether the financial statements give a true and fair view. An opinion that is not 'clean' is a serious warning sign.
An announcement by a company that profit will be lower, or the loss larger, than previously forecast.
The system of rules and checks on how a company is run: the board, auditors, shareholder rights and transparency. Austria has a voluntary Corporate Governance Code.
A deal between a company and people or firms close to it, such as managers, major shareholders or their companies. A reason for extra scrutiny.
The US SEC's free online database of company filings, such as the annual 10-K report.
A period of rising prices and optimism. Investor.gov's general definition: a broad market index rises by 20% or more over at least two months.
A period of falling prices and pessimism. Investor.gov's general definition: a broad market index falls by 20% or more over at least two months.
Market slang for a smaller fall in prices, often around 10%. There is no official definition.
The fall from a peak to a later low, in percent. After a drawdown, a larger percentage gain is needed to recover: −50% needs +100%.
A period when prices rise far above what the underlying income can justify, driven by expectations of further price rises. It ends when the enthusiasm fades, often in a crash.
Using borrowed money to increase the size of an investment or a business. It magnifies gains and losses.
A significant decline in economic activity that is spread across the economy and lasts more than a few months (NBER definition). Media often use two quarters of falling GDP as a rule of thumb.
The recurring pattern of economic expansion, peak, recession and trough.
19 October 1987, when the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 22.6% in one day. The name is also used for 28 October 1929.
The deep, decade-long economic downturn that began in 1929, with a stock market crash and waves of bank failures, and lasted until the Second World War.
A home loan to a borrower with a weak credit history, a small down payment or high payments relative to income. Losses on such loans triggered the 2007–2009 crisis.
A security backed by a pool of home loans; investors receive the payments borrowers make. Such securities spread US mortgage losses through the financial system in 2007–2009.
Large-scale purchases of bonds by a central bank to push down longer-term interest rates when short-term rates are already near zero.
A central bank's public statements about the likely future path of interest rates, used to influence longer-term rates today.
A 1980s strategy that used futures and options to sell automatically as prices fell. It is seen as one cause of the speed of the 1987 crash.
The late-1990s boom in internet and technology shares that peaked in March 2000 and was followed by a long decline.
The 'founders' period' of rapid industrialisation and company formation in Austria-Hungary from 1867 to 1873, which ended with the Vienna stock market crash of 9 May 1873.
The institution that issues a currency and steers its interest rates, such as the ECB for the euro or the Federal Reserve for the US dollar.
The European Central Bank. Its Governing Council sets interest rates for the euro area, aiming for 2% inflation over the medium term.
The ECB together with the national central banks of the euro area countries, including the Oesterreichische Nationalbank.
Austria's central bank and part of the Eurosystem. Its governor represents Austria on the ECB Governing Council.
The central bank of the United States, often called the Fed. Its dual mandate is maximum employment and stable prices.
The two goals set for the US Federal Reserve by Congress: maximum employment and stable prices.
The interest rate banks receive for overnight deposits with the Eurosystem. Since March 2024 it is the rate through which the ECB steers its monetary policy.
The inflation rate a central bank aims for. The ECB aims for 2% (HICP) over the medium term, symmetrically.
Austria's national consumer price index, published by Statistik Austria alongside the EU-harmonised HICP.
The process through which central bank decisions affect interest rates, asset prices, exchange rates, spending and finally inflation, with long and variable delays.
Gross domestic product: the value of all goods and services produced in an economy in a period. Its growth rate is the main measure of economic growth.
An early estimate of an economic figure, such as inflation, published before all data is available and later revised.
The price of one currency in another. The ECB quotes reference rates as units of foreign currency per 1 euro.
The risk that changes in exchange rates reduce the value of a foreign investment in your home currency.
Using derivatives to offset most of the effect of exchange rate changes on a foreign investment. It reduces swings but costs money and removes currency gains.
The return an investor earns on a bond at its current price. When yields rise, the prices of existing bonds fall.
A line showing the yields of bonds from the same issuer across different maturities. It is usually upward sloping; an inverted curve has been a US recession warning sign.
The difference between a long-term and a short-term interest rate, for example the 10-year minus the 1-year government bond yield.
A general fall in prices. It makes debts heavier in real terms and can lead people to postpone spending.
A company's ability to raise prices without losing many customers. It helps profits keep up with inflation.
The tendency of households to spend more when the value of their assets, such as shares, rises, and less when it falls.
The euro area's permanent rescue fund, set up on 8 October 2012 as successor to the temporary EFSF (June 2010), to lend to countries that lose market access.
A crisis in which investors doubt that governments can repay their debts. In the euro area it began in 2010.
An ECB programme announced in September 2012 to buy government bonds in the secondary market, on condition that the country has an EFSF/ESM programme.
The tendency of investors to hold mostly shares and bonds of their own country, which reduces diversification.
How a portfolio is divided among asset categories such as shares, bonds and cash. It depends mainly on your time horizon and risk tolerance.
Bringing a portfolio back to its original asset allocation after some investments have grown faster than others.
The number of months, years or decades you plan to invest before you need the money for a goal.
Your ability and willingness to lose some or all of an investment in exchange for greater potential returns.
Easily accessible savings for unexpected expenses or loss of income, often three to six months of living expenses, so you do not have to sell investments at a bad time.
A diversified fund that automatically shifts towards a more conservative mix as it approaches a set year, its target date.
A planned change in asset allocation over time, usually reducing the share of stocks as a goal such as retirement approaches.
Investing in funds that track an index instead of trying to beat it, usually at low cost.
A short written plan setting out your goals, target mix, products, rebalancing rules and what you will do in a market crash.
A larger amount invested at once, as opposed to regular smaller amounts through a savings plan.
Buying and selling securities within the same day to profit from short price moves. Investor.gov calls it extremely risky; studies find most retail day traders lose money.
Holding positions for days to a few weeks to profit from price swings, often using chart analysis.
A financial instrument whose value is derived from an underlying asset, security or index, such as an option, a future or a CFD.
A contract giving the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy (call) or sell (put) an underlying at a fixed price within or at the end of a set period, in exchange for a premium.
The fixed price at which the holder of an option or warrant can buy or sell the underlying.
The price the buyer of an option pays the seller for the right it gives. It is the most the option buyer can lose.
The seller of an option, who receives the premium and must deliver or buy the underlying if the buyer exercises. Losses can be very large, for uncovered calls even unlimited.
The part of an option's price that reflects the time left until expiry. It shrinks as expiry approaches.
A standardised, exchange-traded agreement that obliges both sides to buy or sell an underlying at a fixed price on a set future date.
A privately agreed, non-standardised contract to buy or sell an asset at a fixed price on a future date; the over-the-counter counterpart of a future.
Collateral deposited to open a futures or other derivatives position. Variation margin settles gains and losses daily, so losing positions require new money.

A leveraged contract with a provider to exchange the difference in an underlying's price between opening and closing. You never own the underlying. In the EU, retail CFDs face leverage limits and negative balance protection.
A bet that pays a fixed amount or nothing depending on whether a condition is met. Their sale to retail clients is banned in Austria by the FMA-PIV.
A rule ensuring that a retail client cannot lose more than the money in their CFD account. Required in the EU and in Austria under the FMA-PIV.
A rapid price rise that forces short sellers to buy back shares to limit losses, which pushes the price up further.
An investor's overall bet on a falling share price. In the EU, positions from 0.1% of share capital must be reported to the regulator and from 0.5% published.
Selling shares short without having borrowed them or arranged to borrow them. Banned for shares in the EU.
Trading on a firm's own account. The FMA warns that paid online prop trading challenges often profit mainly from participants' fees.
The risk that the issuer of a bond, certificate or warrant cannot pay. Certificates are debts of the issuing bank, so you can lose money even if the underlying rises.
The study of how real people make financial decisions, including the systematic errors caused by psychology.
A mental shortcut for making decisions quickly. Useful in daily life, but it can lead to systematic errors in investing.
A systematic error in thinking that affects judgements and decisions, such as loss aversion or overconfidence.
Kahneman and Tversky's theory of how people actually decide under risk, including that losses weigh more heavily than equal gains.
The tendency to feel losses more intensely than gains of the same size, which makes investors focus on avoiding losses.
The tendency to sell winning investments too soon and hold losing investments too long.
The tendency to value something more highly simply because you own it.
Overestimating your own knowledge or skill. In investing it leads to excessive trading and lower returns.
Copying what the majority does instead of deciding on the facts, which amplifies bubbles and panics.
Fear of missing out: the urge to buy because others seem to be making money, often leading to buying near the top.
Judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind, which leads to underestimating risks that have not occurred recently.
Giving more weight to the most recent information than to older information.
Treating money differently depending on which mental 'account' it is in, instead of looking at the overall effect of decisions.
Letting one positive feature, such as a famous brand, colour your whole judgement of an investment.
A change in how choices are presented that makes good decisions easier without forbidding any option, such as automatic enrolment in a savings plan.
A person who shares financial and investing content on social media. Not a protected title; check qualifications and conflicts of interest.
Earning a commission when followers sign up or buy through a personal link, which creates a conflict of interest for the person recommending.
A measure of how widely returns spread around their average; the usual way to express volatility. About two-thirds of outcomes typically fall within one standard deviation.
The gap between the average of yearly returns and the compound return actually earned, caused by swings. +50% then −50% averages 0% but loses 25%.
The constant yearly rate that would turn the starting value into the final value; what your money actually earned per year.
A number from −1 to +1 measuring how closely two investments move together. The lower it is, the more combining them reduces risk.
Excess return over a risk-free benchmark divided by its standard deviation: return per unit of risk.
The return of an investment minus the return of a benchmark, usually a risk-free rate such as short-term government bills.
The return on an investment considered free of default risk, usually short-term government bills, used as a benchmark for other returns.
Risk that affects almost all investments at once, such as recessions or interest rate shocks. It cannot be removed by diversifying across shares.
Risk that affects a single company or sector, such as a failed product or fraud. It can be greatly reduced by diversification.
The risk that you cannot sell an investment when you want, or only at a poor price.
The risk that rising prices erode the purchasing power of your savings and returns, especially for cash and fixed-rate investments.
The risk that changes in interest rates reduce the value of investments, especially bonds with long maturities.
The risk of having too much in one company, sector, country or asset, so that a single failure causes large losses.
Deciding how much money to put into a single investment, for example by capping each position or limiting the amount at risk.
The risk that bad years arrive at the wrong time, such as just before or after you start withdrawing money, permanently reducing the pot.
The 1-to-7 risk scale in a product's Key Information Document, combining market risk (based on volatility) and the issuer's credit risk.
In Austria, the flat rate for most capital income: 27.5%, or 25% for interest on bank deposits. It is applied separately from other income and does not raise the progressive rate.
In Austria, the effect that KESt withheld by a domestic bank or company settles the income tax on that income, so it need not be declared.
In Austria, the option to have all capital income taxed at the normal progressive rate instead of the special rate, useful for people with low total income.
In Austria, setting losses on capital assets against capital income taxed the same way in the same year. Banks do it automatically within their accounts; across banks via the tax return.
Tax deducted at source by the country where income such as a dividend arises. Austrian banks can credit foreign withholding tax on dividends up to 15% of the dividend.
A treaty between two countries that limits taxation of the same income by both, for example by allowing foreign tax to be credited.
In Austria, the acquisition cost used for repeated purchases of the same security in one account: total cost divided by total units, recalculated after each purchase.
In Austria, shares and fund units acquired up to 31 December 2010 (cryptocurrencies up to 28 February 2021), generally exempt from the current tax on gains.
The supplementary form to the Austrian income tax return for declaring capital income, filed via FinanzOnline.
The Austrian tax administration's online portal for filing tax returns and communicating with the tax office.
In Austria, a yearly statement banks must provide on request (from income in 2025, by 31 March) listing capital income, KESt, foreign tax and losses, linked to form E 1kv.
In Austria, the rule that moving abroad is treated like a sale of capital assets at market value; deferral can be requested for moves within the EU/EEA.
The annual exchange of financial account data between tax authorities under the OECD/G20 standard, in place since 2017.
The EU regulation (applicable since 3 July 2016) that defines and bans insider dealing and market manipulation and sets disclosure duties for issuers and managers.
Precise, non-public information about an issuer or financial instrument that would be likely to move the price significantly if made public.
Using inside information to trade, recommending trades on that basis, or passing it on. A criminal and administrative offence in Austria.
Trades, orders or information that give false or misleading signals about supply, demand or price, or set prices at artificial levels.
A scheme in which promoters push up the price of a cheap share with hype or false claims, then sell their own shares at the top, leaving others with losses.
A company announcement publishing inside information without delay, as required by Article 17 MAR, for example a profit warning.
In Austria, the duty to report when voting rights in a listed company reach, exceed or fall below thresholds from 4% to 90%, within two trading days.
Trades by managers of a listed company and their close associates in the company's shares, which must be reported within three business days once €20,000 a year is reached.
In Austria, the obligation to offer to buy all shares after gaining more than 30% of the voting rights in a listed company, at a legally set minimum price.
Austria's independent authority at the Vienna Stock Exchange that supervises takeover offers and decides whether a mandatory offer is required.
In an Austrian stock corporation, the body that runs the company on its own responsibility.
In an Austrian stock corporation, the body that monitors the management board and is elected by the general meeting.
Writing down or converting into shares the claims of a failing bank's shareholders and creditors, so that they, rather than taxpayers, bear its losses.
The orderly restructuring or winding down of a failing bank by a resolution authority, using tools such as sale of business, a bridge bank or bail-in.
In Austria, the Joint Conciliation Board of the Austrian Banking Industry, which mediates complaints about Austrian banks free of charge after you have tried to resolve them with the bank.
Environmental, social and governance factors considered by investors to manage risk or align investments with values.
The EU regulation requiring financial firms to disclose how they consider sustainability risks and adverse impacts, and to justify sustainability claims.
Presenting a product or company as more environmentally friendly or sustainable than it really is.
